She finds that consumers win 88% of cases involving large online retailers but only 41% of cases involving small local traders, though the governing statute and leading precedents make no such distinction. She concludes: 'The doctrine is a fiction; judges decide on sympathy and explain afterwards.' Evaluate her conclusion from the perspectives of American realism, Hart and Dworkin.
markScheme: Identifies the finding as consistent with realist 'stimulus of the facts' (Leiter)
Llewellyn: situation-types and patterns not visible in doctrine
Notes the 88% vs 41% pattern does not by itself show doctrine is a fiction (confounding variables, selection effects)
Considers whether the pattern reflects legitimate legal factors (e.g. bargaining power, standard-form terms, transparency)
Hart: internal point of view; judges guided by rules even when they have discretion in the penumbra
Hart: open texture of terms like 'fair' and 'significant imbalance' allows variation
Dworkin: principles such as inequality of bargaining power may justify outcomes; the pattern could reflect integrity
Dworkin: judges' explanations are part of the law, not post hoc cover
Critique of the 'decide then explain' (hunch) thesis; context of discovery vs justification
Methodological limits of outcome studies
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Okafor's data fit the American realist picture. Leiter reads realism as holding that judges respond chiefly to the stimulus of the facts. Llewellyn urged lawyers to look for situation-types that predict results better than doctrinal categories do. A large gap between online retailers and local traders, unexplained by the statute, is the kind of pattern realists expect. Hutcheson's account of the judicial hunch matches her claim that explanation follows decision.

Her conclusion still overreaches. Statistically, outcome rates depend on which cases are litigated and appealed. Retailers may settle strong cases and fight weak ones, while local traders may appeal only where they have good arguments. The pattern also may track legally relevant factors. Large online retailers typically use non-negotiated standard terms drafted by lawyers and buried in long documents. Unfair terms legislation usually directs attention to transparency, prominence and imbalance, all of which may differ systematically between the two groups.

Hart would locate any real variation in the open texture of evaluative terms such as 'fair' or 'significant imbalance'. In penumbral cases judges exercise discretion, and patterns in that discretion are unsurprising. But they still treat the statute as a standard from the internal point of view. Their explanations are not mere decoration.

Dworkin would go further and argue the pattern may express law as integrity. Principles about inequality of bargaining power and protection of the weaker party fit consumer law's structure and justify treating large retailers more strictly. On this view the outcomes are not in spite of doctrine but are its best interpretation.

The realist insight remains valuable. The pattern may reveal unstated assumptions that ought to be examined openly. The distinction between the context of discovery and the context of justification answers the 'explain afterwards' charge. Even if intuition comes first, the duty to give reasons constrains which intuitions survive.

Conclusion: the data justify closer scrutiny of how open-textured standards are applied, not the claim that doctrine is a fiction.

questions.q: Explain and assess Dworkin's distinction between arguments of principle and arguments of policy, and its implications for the judicial role.
markScheme: Defines principle (individual rights) and policy (collective goals)
Rights as trumps
Courts should decide hard cases on principle; legislatures may pursue policy
Democratic argument: unelected judges should not set collective goals
Argument from retroactivity: deciding on principle enforces existing rights
Example of a case presented as principle (e.g. negligence or nervous shock in McLoughlin v O'Brian)
Criticism: the distinction is hard to draw; policy considerations pervade English negligence law (e.g. Caparo 'fair, just and reasonable')
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Dworkin distinguished arguments of principle, which establish individual rights, from arguments of policy, which justify decisions as advancing a collective goal. Rights are trumps: they defeat appeals to aggregate welfare.

He argued courts should decide hard cases on principle. Two reasons support this. First, democracy: elected legislatures are better placed to weigh competing interests in pursuit of collective goals, while unelected judges should confine themselves to rights. Second, retroactivity: when a judge decides on principle, she enforces a right the winning party already had, so the decision is not an unfair change of rules after the event. A policy decision would impose new burdens retrospectively.

In Law's Empire Dworkin used McLoughlin v O'Brian [1983] 1 AC 410 to illustrate. Lord Scarman's speech, stressing principle and leaving policy-based limits to Parliament, contrasted with Lord Wilberforce's readiness to draw limits on policy grounds.

The distinction faces difficulties. English negligence law openly uses policy. Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605 asks whether imposing a duty is fair, just and reasonable, and floodgates arguments are common. Dworkin might reply that many such arguments can be recast as principles about fairness to defendants. Critics say this makes the distinction depend on description. Also, rights themselves often presuppose views about collective welfare.

The distinction is better seen as an ideal of judicial justification than as a description of practice. It usefully reminds judges that their legitimacy rests on reasoning from rights embedded in the law.
